title: The world, reviewed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the life cycle, and your line: every stage. A call in a newborn's ear, a prayer with no call before it. Who did you reach at a hard stage? Day one thousand four hundred nineteen.

"The difference of your languages and colours." That phrase sits in the Qur'an's list of Allah's signs, right beside the creation of the heavens and the earth. Languages and colors, counted as signs, like mountains and rain. Hold that next to the last stretch of this year. A circle of Sufi chanting in Senegal. A youth group studying online on a weeknight. A Shia family in a hall of mourning in a big city. A convert at her first Friday prayer. An imam in a small town who leads the prayer and then helps stack the chairs. Today, the world again: a diverse, living ummah.
screen: `LANGUAGES AND COLORS, AS SIGNS.` → `SENEGAL, ONLINE, A FIRST FRIDAY.` → `A DIVERSE, LIVING UMMAH.`

segments.voice: First, the variety the year met. It described each group in its own words and ranked none. The Deobandi and Barelvi traditions of South Asia. The traveling preachers of the Tablighi Jamaat. The Salafi approach, which seeks to follow the earliest generations closely, and is itself diverse. Sufi orders like the Tijaniyyah and the Muridiyyah. Shia communities in Iraq, Lebanon, Iran and beyond, and the Isma'ilis with their living Imam. Converts, some of whom prefer the word reverts. Women speaking for themselves, and not all agreeing. Young people, and Muslims living as minorities. Second, why variety is not a problem in the text. The Qur'an says people were made into nations and tribes, in Pickthall's words, "that ye may know one another." Not that they may be identical. That they may meet and learn each other. Third, what holds it together. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, says the believers in their mercy and love for one another are like one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. Not one uniform. One body, with many parts that feel each other's pain. Fourth, what that asks of an ordinary day. A body knows about its far limbs. A Muslim in Ohio hearing about a flood in Bangladesh, or a mosque fire in a town she will never visit, is being asked by that hadith to feel it. The ummah is less a map than a nervous system.
screen: `MANY WAYS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.` · `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · `LIKE ONE BODY.` · `LESS A MAP THAN A NERVOUS SYSTEM.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for Muslims everywhere. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Travel slowly, one breath per place. A mosque near you. A city in West Africa. A town in South Asia. A village in Indonesia. A family in a refugee camp. A student far from home. A convert praying alone in a small apartment. If you pray, you can ask good for them in your own words. If you don't, simply let each place be real for a breath, full of people waking, working and praying. The bell holds the time.
The world. The ummah, the worldwide community of Muslims, many languages and colors, one body in the hadith's picture. Today's word.

Your line: everywhere. Today, read one piece of news about Muslims in a place far from you, and let it reach you the way an ache reaches the rest of the body. Tomorrow, what surprised you. Day one thousand four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims pray for the wider ummah in their own words, and send aid to Muslim communities hit by disaster, sometimes through their local mosque.

original.note: Arabic: a community or nation; the ummah is the community of Muslims.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Muslim world is one place with one culture.
what it means: a community in many languages, colors and schools, pictured in the hadith as one body.
what a scholar hears: 30:22 on languages and colors as signs, 49:13's li-ta'arafu, that ye may know one another, and Bukhari's one body.

notes: Confirm Pickthall's wording of 30:22 ('the difference of your languages and colours') and 49:13 ('that ye may know one another').
The groups listed recall days 1367–1380 and are described without counts or ranking; a Keeper should confirm each one-line description is fair, especially the Salafi and Isma'ili lines.
'A Muslim in Ohio... a flood in Bangladesh' is an illustration, not a reported event.
li-ta'arafu (49:13) in the trapdoor: confirm transliteration.
